Appendix D Consistent Probe–Readout R2R^{2} Gap Under MSE Loss


In Table˜1, we reported a substantial gap between the hidden-state probe R2R^{2} and the linear head R2R^{2} at ω=365\omega=365. Figure˜2 shows that this gap persists across all volatility periods ω∈{30,90,178,365,730}\omega\in\{30,90,178,365,730\} for both the Transformer and the MLP under MSE training. For both architectures, the hidden probe R2R^{2} is consistently higher than the linear head R2R^{2}. The gap narrows as ω\omega increases, and both probe R2R^{2} and head R2R^{2} improve with longer volatility cycles. The Transformer exhibits a consistently smaller alignment gap than the MLP, especially at ω=30\omega=30 and ω=90\omega=90, suggesting that under MSE training its learned head remains better aligned with the latent-state direction encoded in the hidden representation.


Figure 2: Probe R2R^{2} and linear head R2R^{2} for decoding 𝒉T+1\bm{h}_{T+1} from the final representation under MSE training, shown across volatility periods for the Transformer and MLP (median over n=10n=10 seeds). In both architectures, probe R2R^{2} remains above head R2R^{2} across all periods, with smaller in long-cycle regimes. The R2R^{2} in Transformer are consistently higher.

Appendix E Less Structured Emergence in the MLP


In the Transformer, the stage at which the latent state 𝒉T+1\bm{h}_{T+1} first becomes linearly decodable depends strongly on the volatility cycle as shown in Figure˜1. This stage-specific pattern is much less pronounced in a standard MLP. As shown in Figure˜3, latent-state decodability in the MLP typically arises in a more diffuse and less modular manner than the Transformer. It arises after the first nonlinear block and then improves more gradually across subsequent layers, rather than emerging sharply at architecture-specific components.


Figure 3: Stage-wise ridge probe R2R^{2} for decoding 𝒉T+1\bm{h}_{T+1} from intermediate MLP representations across volatility periods. Unlike the Transformer, the MLP exhibits a smoother and less localized rise in decodability, with weaker dependence on volatility period.


We also consider an MLP control with an ℓ2\ell^{2}-normalization layer inserted after the initial linear embedding, mirroring the corresponding preprocessing step in the Transformer. As shown in Figure˜4, this normalized MLP exhibits a similar pattern: in long-cycle regimes, the linear embedding together with ℓ2\ell^{2}-normalization accounts for most of the decodability of ht+1h_{t+1}. As ω\omega decreases, the dominant contribution shifts from ℓ2\ell^{2}-normalization alone to a shared contribution from ℓ2\ell^{2}-normalization and the subsequent nonlinear activation.


Figure 4: Stage-wise ridge probe R2R^{2} for decoding 𝒉T+1\bm{h}_{T+1} in an MLP with ℓ2\ell^{2} normalization after the initial linear layer.

Appendix F Stage-Wise Results for Two-Layer Transformers


We also examine whether a deeper Transformer exhibits a different stage-wise emergence pattern. Figure˜5 shows that the main decodability transitions still occur in the first layer. In our setting, increasing depth from one layer to two does not substantially change where the latent-state representation is formed.


Figure 5: Stage-wise ridge probe R2R^{2} for decoding hT+1h_{T+1} from intermediate representations in a two-layer Transformer across volatility periods. The main gains in decodability occur before or within the first layer, while the second layer yields only limited additional improvement.

Appendix G Impact of Signal-to-Noise Ratio


The spectral radius ρ\rho of the state-transition matrix AA controls the persistence of the latent process 𝒉t\bm{h}_{t}, and hence its signal-to-noise ratio. Smaller ρ\rho leads to faster decay and weaker recoverable structure, while ρ\rho near 11 yields more persistent dynamics and higher latent-state decodability. Consistent with this, ridge probe R2R^{2} rises sharply as ρ\rho increases and then largely plateaus for the largest values; representative trajectories are shown in Figure˜6, with quantitative results in Table˜3.

Causal perturbation of the post-norm representation.


We next test whether the post-ℓ2\ell^{2}-norm embedding is causally upstream of the forecast. Following causal intervention methods from mechanistic interpretability, in the spirit of activation patching, causal tracing and concept-erasure [Meng et al., 2022, Heimersheim and Nanda, 2024, Belrose et al., 2023], we remove a varying fraction α\alpha of the component aligned with the latent-state direction at a chosen stage and then propagate the perturbed activation through the remainder of the network unchanged. We apply this intervention to the post-input-embedding, post-ℓ2\ell^{2}-norm, post-positional-embedding, post-attention, and post-FFN representations, and measure both the downstream change in latent-state decodability (Figure˜1) and the change in forecast error (Figure˜7). For ω=365\omega=365, perturbing the post-ℓ2\ell^{2}-norm representation produces the largest downstream collapse in decodability and the strongest increase in forecast MSE and MAE, whereas perturbations at later stages have substantially weaker effects. This identifies the ℓ2\ell^{2}-normalized embedding as the earliest stage at which the latent-state signal becomes causally relevant for the model’s prediction.
